subject: computing
subtitle: Breaking problems into sub-problems and removing irrelevant detail.

data.targetWord: a structured approach to problem-solving used in computer science, involving decomposition, abstraction, pattern recognition, and algorithm design

examples.en-GB: Computational thinking helps programmers break down complex problems before writing any code.

data.targetWord: breaking a large, complex problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems that are each easier to understand, solve, and test

examples.en-GB: Using decomposition, a programmer splits a school website project into layout, content, navigation, and testing tasks.

data.targetWord: a smaller, more manageable part of a larger problem created by applying decomposition

examples.en-GB: Designing the navigation menu is one sub-problem when building a school website.

data.targetWord: designing software as a collection of self-contained, reusable modules or subroutines, each solving one sub-problem

examples.en-GB: Modular design allowed the team to assign each sub-problem to a different programmer.

data.targetWord: a named, self-contained block of code that performs a specific task and can be called from other parts of a program

examples.en-GB: The subroutine calculateAverageScore() is called once for each student without repeating the calculation logic.

data.targetWord: removing unnecessary or irrelevant detail from a problem or model so that only the important features remain

examples.en-GB: A map uses abstraction by showing roads as lines and omitting details like road texture or the presence of people.

data.targetWord: a simplified representation of a real-world system that emphasises relevant features and hides irrelevant ones

examples.en-GB: A road map is a model of the real landscape, showing only what a traveller needs.

data.targetWord: the visible part of a subroutine or system — its name, inputs, and outputs — which hides the internal implementation detail

examples.en-GB: The interface of calculateArea(length, width) shows what goes in and what comes out, without revealing how the calculation is done.

data.targetWord: bundling data and the code that processes it inside a single unit so that internal details are hidden from outside code

examples.en-GB: Encapsulation means the variable playerScore is only modified through the approved functions, not directly from anywhere in the program.

data.targetWord: a design approach that starts with the overall problem and repeatedly decomposes it into smaller sub-problems until each is simple enough to code

examples.en-GB: Using top-down design, the programmer first defined the main modules, then broke each one into smaller tasks.

data.targetWord: a self-contained unit of code that performs one specific function and can be developed and tested independently

examples.en-GB: Each module in the library program handled one task: storing books, searching, or recording loans.

data.targetWord: creating a solution broad enough to apply to many similar problems, not just the specific case it was first written for

examples.en-GB: A calculateArea(length, width) function is a generalisation — it works for any rectangle, not just one specific size.

data.targetWord: the ability of a piece of code or module to be used in multiple programs or multiple places in the same program without rewriting it

examples.en-GB: Good reusability means the validateInput() subroutine can be used in the student record system and the library system.

data.targetWord: a named storage location in a program that holds a value, abstracting away the underlying memory address and binary representation

examples.en-GB: The variable score holds the player's points without the programmer needing to know which memory address stores it.

data.targetWord: application programming interface — a set of abstracted functions that lets programmers use a service without knowing its internal workings

examples.en-GB: Using a weather API, the programmer requests forecast data without understanding how the weather server collects or stores it.

data.targetWord: a problem-solving strategy where a problem is split into smaller independent sub-problems, each solved separately, then combined

examples.en-GB: Divide and conquer is why teams of programmers can work on different modules of the same application simultaneously.

data.targetWord: a level in a computer system that hides the complexity of the layer below and provides a simpler interface to the layer above

examples.en-GB: The operating system is an abstraction layer between application software and the physical hardware.

data.targetWord: system software that abstracts the hardware and provides a standard interface for application programs to run on any compatible computer

examples.en-GB: Because of the operating system, a programmer can write to a file without knowing which physical disk sectors store the data.

data.targetWord: a hierarchical diagram that shows how a problem is broken down into sub-problems, with the main problem at the top and sub-problems branching below

examples.en-GB: The decomposition tree for the quiz app showed three main branches: load questions, run quiz loop, and show results.

data.targetWord: a finite, unambiguous sequence of steps designed to solve a problem or complete a task

examples.en-GB: The algorithm for checking a student's score and awarding a grade was tested before being translated into code.

data.targetWord: a subroutine that performs a specific task and returns a value to the part of the program that called it

examples.en-GB: The function calculateTax(income) takes an income value and returns the tax owed.

data.targetWord: the practice of concealing the internal workings of a module so that other parts of the program only interact with its interface

examples.en-GB: Information hiding means a programmer can change how sendEmail() works internally without affecting any code that calls it.

data.targetWord: testing each module or sub-problem separately to confirm it works correctly before combining it with the rest of the program

examples.en-GB: Independent testing let the team find the bug in the calculateScore() module before it affected the whole program.

data.targetWord: information that is needed for the task at hand and must be kept in the abstract model or representation

examples.en-GB: On a tube map, station names and connections are relevant detail; the exact curves of the tunnels are not.

data.targetWord: information that is not needed for the current task and should be removed during abstraction to create a cleaner model

examples.en-GB: The texture of road surfaces is irrelevant detail on a navigation map and is therefore abstracted away.

data.targetWord: a real-world example of abstraction: it shows only the information the driver needs (speed, fuel, temperature) and hides thousands of underlying sensor readings

examples.en-GB: A car dashboard abstracts away engine diagnostics and shows only speed and fuel level.

data.targetWord: the process by which a map removes three-dimensional, textural, and human detail from the real world to produce a navigable two-dimensional representation

examples.en-GB: Map abstraction converts physical tarmac roads into simple lines so travellers can plan routes easily.

data.targetWord: how easily a program can be updated, corrected, or extended after it is first written, improved by decomposition into independent modules

examples.en-GB: Good maintainability means fixing a bug in the displayResults() module does not require changes anywhere else.

data.targetWord: the ability of a system to grow and handle more work without requiring a complete redesign, made possible by well-decomposed modular structure

examples.en-GB: Because the social media platform was well decomposed into modules, adding a stories feature required only a new module.

data.targetWord: a real-world example where a cash machine presents a simple touchscreen interface while hiding secure bank authentication, server communication, and note-counting mechanisms

examples.en-GB: ATM abstraction means a user withdraws cash by tapping buttons, completely unaware of the authentication and server requests happening underneath.

data.sentence: Breaking a complex problem into smaller, more manageable parts is called ____.
Removing unnecessary detail from a problem so that only important features remain is called ____.
A smaller part created by breaking down a large problem is called a ____.
Decomposition allows different programmers to work on different sub-problems ____, saving time on large projects.
In programming, decomposition is implemented using ____, which are named blocks of code that each solve one sub-problem.
A map is an example of abstraction because it removes ____ detail such as road texture and the presence of people.
A car ____ abstracts away thousands of sensor readings and shows only speed, fuel level, and engine temperature.
When a programmer writes score = 10, the variable name abstracts away the underlying binary ____ address.
A subroutine's name, inputs, and outputs form its ____, which is all that other parts of the program need to know.
An API is an example of abstraction because it lets programmers use a service without understanding its ____ workings.
Designing software as a collection of self-contained, reusable sub-programs is called ____ design.
One benefit of decomposition is that if a bug is found in one module, only that ____ needs to be fixed.
A completed subroutine can be ____ in other projects, saving development time.
The operating system is an abstraction ____ that sits between application software and the physical hardware.
Decomposition and abstraction are always used together: decomposition divides the problem and abstraction ____ unnecessary detail within each part.

data.title: Steps to decompose a problem into a program
data.instruction: Put these stages of the decomposition process in the correct order.
items: Break the problem into major sub-problems
Break each sub-problem into smaller tasks
Write a subroutine for each task
Combine subroutines into the complete program

data.title: Layers of abstraction in a computer system
data.instruction: Put these layers in order from the highest abstraction (user-facing) to the lowest (physical hardware).
items: User — sees icons, windows, and menus
Application software — uses OS functions and file system
Hardware — physical circuits and electrical signals
